Visualizing spectral variation

Jose Eduardo Meireles

July 2026

  • Coloring spectra by a grouping (base R)
  • The tidy path: ggplot2
  • Spectral redundancy: band autocorrelation
  • Dominant axes: PCA
  • Data note

A single reflectance curve is easy to read; a few hundred of them stacked on one plot are not. This vignette is about seeing variation: coloring spectra by a grouping, summarizing spread with quantile bands, exposing the strong band-to-band redundancy that makes spectra behave like a handful of underlying signals, and extracting the dominant axes of variation with PCA. It uses both the base-R plotting in spectrolab and the tidy/ggplot2 bridge (to_long(), as_tibble(), autoplot()).

Throughout we use the built-in spec_matrix_example, a simulated dataset of 50 spectra whose sample names encode 10 “species” – a convenient stand-in for a categorical grouping.

s = as_spectra(spec_matrix_example, name_idx = 1)
dim(s)                     # 50 samples x 2101 bands (400-2500 nm)
#> n_samples   n_bands 
#>        50      2101
length(unique(names(s)))   # 10 groups, carried in the sample names
#> [1] 10

The _common.R helper (sourced above) supplies the shared visual language used in every vignette: a colorblind-safe categorical palette (spec_pal), sequential/diverging ramps (spec_seq(), spec_div()), light region tints (spec_region_tints), a ggplot2 theme (theme_spectra()), and two grouping helpers. species_cols(x) returns a per-sample color vector; group_palette(x) returns the same mapping plus the named palette and levels needed to build a legend. Both cap the grouping at 8 colors and fold the rest into "Other".

Coloring spectra by a grouping (base R)

The workhorse is plot.spectra(). Passing a per-sample color vector from species_cols() turns an undifferentiated tangle of lines into a group-structured one. We shade the canonical spectral regions underneath with plot_regions() and build a legend from the named palette in group_palette().

gp = group_palette(s)

plot(s, col = species_cols(s), lwd = 1, ylab = "reflectance",
     xlab = "wavelength (nm)")
plot_regions(s, col = spec_region_tints)
legend("topleft", legend = names(gp$pal), col = gp$pal,
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8, ncol = 2)

Even colored, 50 overlapping curves hide the within-group spread. A cleaner summary draws each group as a shaded quantile band instead of individual lines. We map every sample back to its (folded) group, then loop, calling plot_quantile(add = TRUE) on each subset with a translucent fill of that group’s color.

grp_of = stats::setNames(names(gp$pal)[match(gp$cols, gp$pal)], names(s))

plot(s, type = "n", ylab = "reflectance", xlab = "wavelength (nm)")
plot_regions(s, col = spec_region_tints)

for(g in names(gp$pal)){
    idx = which(grp_of == g)
    if(length(idx) >= 2){
        plot_quantile(s[idx, ], total_prob = 0.9, add = TRUE, border = FALSE,
                      col = grDevices::adjustcolor(gp$pal[[g]], 0.25))
    }
}
legend("topleft", legend = names(gp$pal), fill = gp$pal, bty = "n",
       cex = 0.8, ncol = 2, border = NA)

Each band spans the central 90% of its group’s reflectance at every wavelength. Overlapping bands mean the groups are not cleanly separable there; narrow, non-overlapping bands (e.g. the red edge near 700 nm) mark the wavelengths that best discriminate the groups.

The tidy path: ggplot2

For grammar-of-graphics workflows, reshape to long format with to_long() (base R, no tidyverse required) and hand the result to ggplot2. Long format carries sample_name, band, and value; we add a stable per-spectrum id (sample names repeat across the 5 replicates per group, so grouping lines by name alone would connect unrelated samples) and the folded group so colors and legend match the base-R plots above.

long         = to_long(s)
long$id      = rep(seq_len(nrow(s)), times = ncol(s))
long$species = rep(grp_of, times = ncol(s))

ggplot2::ggplot(long, ggplot2::aes(band, value, group = id, colour = species)) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.3) +
    ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = group_palette(s)$pal) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "wavelength (nm)", y = "reflectance", colour = NULL) +
    theme_spectra()

Because the long data is a plain data.frame, the rest of the grammar composes normally. facet_wrap() breaks the overplotted bundle into small multiples – one panel per group, which reads far better than a single crowded axis.

ggplot2::ggplot(long, ggplot2::aes(band, value, group = id, colour = species)) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = group_palette(s)$pal) +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ sample_name) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "wavelength (nm)", y = "reflectance") +
    theme_spectra()

The ggplot2 equivalent of the shaded quantile band is geom_ribbon(). Compute per-band quantiles with quantile() – which returns one spectrum per probability – then plot the outer probabilities as a ribbon and the median as a line.

qt  = quantile(s, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
qv  = value(qt)
fan = data.frame(band = bands(qt), lo = qv[1, ], mid = qv[2, ], hi = qv[3, ])

ggplot2::ggplot(fan, ggplot2::aes(band)) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
                         fill = spec_pal[1], alpha = 0.25) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = mid), colour = spec_pal[1], linewidth = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "wavelength (nm)", y = "reflectance",
                  title = "Median and 5-95% band") +
    theme_spectra()

For a one-liner default, autoplot(s) draws all spectra as a bare ggplot object you can extend. Note that autoplot() drops metadata, so it cannot color by a grouping on its own – when you need groups, go through to_long() as above and add the color aesthetic yourself.

ggplot2::autoplot(s) + theme_spectra()

Spectral redundancy: band autocorrelation

Adjacent bands measure almost the same thing, which is why a 2101-band spectrum carries far fewer than 2101 independent numbers. The band-by-band correlation matrix makes this concrete. A full-resolution cor() would be a 2101x2101 matrix – needless compute and a multi-megabyte figure – so we first downsample to ~10 nm resolution with resample().

sc = resample(s, seq(400, 2400, by = 10), fwhm = 10)   # ~200 bands
M  = cor(as.matrix(sc))
wl = bands(sc)

op = graphics::par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
image(x = wl, y = wl, z = M, zlim = c(-1, 1),
      col = spec_div(255), useRaster = TRUE,
      xlab = "wavelength (nm)", ylab = "wavelength (nm)")

graphics::par(op)

The diverging palette is centered at zero (zlim = c(-1, 1)): blue is positive correlation, red negative, pale neutral near zero. The image is dominated by large blocks of near-perfect positive correlation – the visible (400-700 nm), the NIR plateau (~800-1300 nm), and the SWIR regions – separated by the water absorption features and the red edge, where correlation drops or flips sign. This block structure is exactly why a few components can reconstruct a spectrum almost perfectly, which the next section exploits.

Dominant axes: PCA

Principal component analysis rotates the band axes into a new set of orthogonal axes ordered by the variance they explain. Because spectra are so redundant, the first two or three components typically capture the overwhelming majority of the variation. We run prcomp() on the sample-by-band matrix.

pca = prcomp(as.matrix(s), center = TRUE)
imp = summary(pca)$importance
round(imp[, 1:5], 4)
#>                           PC1    PC2    PC3    PC4    PC5
#> Standard deviation     0.3743 0.1152 0.0321 0.0041 0.0018
#> Proportion of Variance 0.9072 0.0859 0.0067 0.0001 0.0000
#> Cumulative Proportion  0.9072 0.9932 0.9998 1.0000 1.0000
ve  = round(imp[2, 1:2] * 100, 1)   # % variance explained by PC1, PC2
ve
#>  PC1  PC2 
#> 90.7  8.6

A score scatter of PC1 versus PC2 places each sample in this reduced space; coloring by group shows how the axes relate to the categorical structure.

lab = paste0(c("PC1", "PC2"), " (", ve, "%)")

op = graphics::par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], col = species_cols(s), pch = 19,
     xlab = lab[1], ylab = lab[2])
legend("topright", legend = names(gp$pal), col = gp$pal, pch = 19,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8, ncol = 2)

graphics::par(op)

The scores tell you where samples sit; the loadings tell you which wavelengths build each axis. Plotting pca$rotation over wavelength – a “loadings-as-spectra” view – reveals the spectral fingerprint of each component. We set up an empty plotting frame, shade the regions, then overlay the first two loading vectors.

rot = pca$rotation[, 1:2]
wl2 = bands(s)

op = graphics::par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(wl2, rot, type = "n", xlab = "wavelength (nm)", ylab = "loading")
plot_regions(s, col = spec_region_tints)
graphics::abline(h = 0, col = spec_muted, lty = 3)
graphics::matlines(wl2, rot, col = c(spec_pal[1], spec_pal[6]), lty = 1, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = lab, col = c(spec_pal[1], spec_pal[6]),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

graphics::par(op)

Peaks and troughs in a loading mark the bands that drive that component; a loading flat near zero means those wavelengths contribute nothing to that axis. Reading the scores and loadings together – which samples separate along an axis, and which wavelengths define it – is the core of interpreting spectral variation.

Data note

spec_matrix_example is simulated. Real reflectance would show cleaner, more textbook structure – sharper water-absorption features, a crisper red edge, and correlation blocks that align even more tightly with the pigment, water, and dry-matter absorptions that organize plant spectra. The workflow, however, is identical on measured data.
